c.tagline: Basque beach city where pintxos, La Concha, and Michelin stars meet.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; Uber does not operate here, but Cabify and Free Now let you book a licensed taxi by app.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Parte Vieja (Old Town): Plaza de la Constitución ringed by famed pintxo bars
hood_landmark.Gros: Zurriola beach, the city's surf strand, beside the Kursaal
hood_landmark.Antiguo: Ondarreta beach below Monte Igueldo and its funicular

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the crowded Parte Vieja pintxo bars and La Concha beach in high summer.

hood_desc: The lively old town wedged between La Concha bay and Monte Urgull, packed with 100-plus pintxo bars, the Santa María basilica, and the Bretxa market; the buzzing first-timer base that comes alive every evening.

The elegant 19th-century Romantic Area of grand Belle Époque buildings, the La Concha promenade, the cathedral, and upscale shopping; refined and central, right by the beach yet quieter than the old town at night.
A trendy, youthful district across the Urumea river fronting surf-friendly Zurriola beach and the cubic Kursaal centre, full of laid-back pintxo bars, sunny terraces, and pedestrian streets.
A relaxed residential neighbourhood at the western end of the bay by quieter Ondarreta beach and the funicular up Monte Igueldo; good for families wanting calm and sea air away from the crowds.
A modern, mostly residential quarter around the Anoeta stadium and the Euskotren hub, with everyday local prices, parks along the Urumea, and easy transport links; a practical, affordable base.
lodging: Hotel de Londres y de Inglaterra

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality throughout the Basque Country.

transit.hours: Dbus city buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM, with a limited Búho night-bus network on weekends; the Euskotren 'Topo' line runs until around 11:00 PM.
transit.note: San Sebastián has no metro or tram; the Dbus bus network covers the compact city, complemented by the Euskotren 'Topo' narrow-gauge line linking Amara to Hendaye (France) and the wider Basque coast.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash on Dbus buses (~€1.85) or tap a rechargeable Mugi transport card for discounted fares; the Mugi card also works on Euskotren and regional Lurraldebus services.

sys.n: Dbus (Compañía del Tranvía de San Sebastián)

transit.m: Lurraldebus E21 bus to city center (~35-45 min)

tip.r: Not expected; locals round up or leave small change, and 5-10% for good service in restaurants is generous.

food.name: Gilda pintxo
food.desc: The original pintxo: a skewer of salt-cured anchovy, pickled guindilla pepper and olive, named for the Rita Hayworth film - salty, green and spicy.

places.name: Casa Vallés
places.note: Claims the invention of the gilda in the 1940s; still an old-school standing bar with excellent txakoli.

places.name: Bar Txepetxa
places.note: Anchovy specialist where the gilda sits beside a dozen dressed anchovy pintxos.

places.name: Bar Martinez
places.note: Small, unpretentious bar near the port; classic cold pintxos and a good stop early in a crawl.

food.name: Txuleta
food.desc: A thick bone-in chop from an old dairy cow, salted and seared over embers so the crust chars while the inside stays rare and mineral-rich.

places.name: Bar Néstor
places.note: One tortilla and a handful of txuletas per service; put your name down when the doors open or miss out.

places.name: Casa Urola
places.note: Pintxo bar downstairs, restaurant upstairs; grilled txuleta and seasonal Basque cooking both excellent.

places.name: Asador Portuetxe
places.note: Out-of-centre grill house where locals go for a full-size txuleta and grilled turbot.

food.name: Bacalao al pil-pil
food.desc: Salt cod poached gently in olive oil and garlic until its gelatine emulsifies into a glossy, shivering sauce - Basque cooking at its most technical.

places.name: Casa Urola
places.note: Kitchen-driven pintxos; cod done both pil-pil and grilled, plus a strong Basque wine list.

places.name: Bar Zeruko
places.note: Famous for La Hoguera, cod smoked at the table over a tiny brazier; theatrical but genuinely good.

places.name: La Cuchara de San Telmo
places.note: No-display kitchen bar; order cod or the veal cheek from the chalkboard and stand with the crowd.

food.name: Anchoa pintxos
food.desc: Cantabrian anchovies, either salt-cured or vinegar-cured boquerones, laid over bread with sea urchin, crab, apple or spider crab dressings.

places.name: Bar Txepetxa
places.note: Family bar that built its name on anchovies alone; the sea urchin and spider crab versions are the ones to get.

places.name: Bar Bergara
places.note: Pioneering pintxo bar across the river, less crowded than Old Town and consistently high quality.

places.name: La Cepa
places.note: Hams hanging from the beams, anchovies and Iberico cut to order in a bar that has been going since 1948.

food.name: Hongos a la plancha
food.desc: Wild mushrooms griddled in olive oil with nothing but salt and a raw egg yolk to stir through - a showcase for Basque produce in autumn.

places.name: Ganbara
places.note: The definitive mushroom pintxo, piled high on the counter; expensive, worth it, go early.

places.name: Bar Zeruko
places.note: Creative counter where mushrooms appear in season alongside more experimental pintxos.

places.name: Bodega Donostiarra
places.note: Neighbourhood favourite for simple griddled plates and tortilla away from the Old Town crush.

food.name: Basque burnt cheesecake
food.desc: Crustless cheesecake baked hot until the top scorches and the centre stays molten - invented here in the 1990s and copied worldwide.

places.name: La Viña
places.note: The birthplace; cheesecakes cooling on the bar all day, best eaten warm with a glass of sweet wine.

places.name: Restaurante Narru
places.note: Modern Basque kitchen doing a refined version of the tarta de queso as a plated dessert.

places.name: Bodega Donostiarra
places.note: Casual bar version of the cheesecake, easy to get without queueing in the Old Town.

food.name: Txakoli
food.desc: Bone-dry, slightly fizzy Basque white poured from a height to aerate it; low in alcohol and made for cutting through anchovies and fried food.

places.name: Ganbara
places.note: Poured properly from a height with every pintxo; the standard measure is a small glass, so keep moving.

places.name: Casa Urola
places.note: Deep list of Getariako Txakolina and Basque whites by the glass.

places.name: Casa Vallés
places.note: Old-fashioned bar with a serious cellar; a calm place to actually taste rather than gulp.

food.name: Sagardoa (Basque cider)
food.desc: Still, sour farmhouse cider caught in a thin stream straight from the barrel at the cry of txotx, drunk standing between courses of cod and txuleta.

places.name: Sidrería Petritegi
places.note: Best-known cider house 15 minutes from town; txotx season runs roughly January to April, book ahead.

places.name: Zelaia Sagardotegia
places.note: Family cider house with the classic set menu of cod omelette, cod pil-pil, txuleta and cheese with quince.

places.name: Astarbe Sagardotegia
places.note: Hillside farm cidery with its own orchards and rooms; quieter than the big-name houses.

landmarks: La Concha Beach & Bay
A perfect shell-shaped crescent of golden sand framed by an elegant belle-epoque balustrade, routinely ranked among Europe's finest urban beaches.
Parte Vieja (Old Town)
The world's densest concentration of pintxo bars crams these narrow streets, making an evening txikiteo crawl the city's essential ritual.
Monte Igueldo
A creaky 1912 funicular climbs to a nostalgic hilltop funfair whose terrace serves the definitive postcard panorama of La Concha Bay.
Peine del Viento (Wind Comb)
Eduardo Chillida's three steel claws grip wave-battered rocks at the bay's western tip, Spain's most celebrated marriage of sculpture and sea.
Monte Urgull
Wooded paths wind past castle ramparts to the Sacred Heart statue crowning this harbour-guarding hill, with history exhibits and stellar viewpoints.
Basílica de Santa María del Coro
The Old Town's theatrical Baroque basilica, its ornate portal perfectly aligned down Calle Mayor with the cathedral's Gothic spire.
Catedral del Buen Pastor
A soaring neo-Gothic cathedral from 1897 whose 75-metre spire, the city's tallest structure, anchors the elegant Ensanche district.
Palacio de Miramar
The English-cottage-style summer palace of Spain's royals presides over lawns sloping to the sea between La Concha and Ondarreta beaches.
Zurriola Beach
Across the river in Gros, this surf-pounded strand fizzes with boards, beach bars and the angular Kursaal congress cubes behind it.
Isla de Santa Clara
A tiny wooded island moored mid-bay with a lighthouse, seasonal ferry and pocket beach that appears only at low tide.

train.note: San Sebastián has a genuine cross-border train: Euskotren's E2 'Topo' line runs from Amara station through Irún to Hendaye in France every half hour, where you change onto SNCF TER services for Bayonne, Bordeaux and the TGV to Paris. Renfe long-distance trains from the separate Estación del Norte reach Madrid in about 5h20 and Barcelona in 6 hours. The two stations are a 15-minute walk apart.

bus.note: The bus station sits underneath the Renfe Estación del Norte across the river from the old town. Coaches reach Bilbao in about an hour and Biarritz in 1h15, and are usually quicker and cheaper than the train. Bring your passport for French routes even though this is an internal Schengen crossing.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from San Sebastián - the small harbour by the old town handles fishing boats and summer launches out to Santa Clara island in the bay. The nearest international sailings are Brittany Ferries' Bilbao-Portsmouth route, about 100 km west.

half.name: Hondarribia
half.blurb: A fishing town on the French border with a walled old quarter of brightly painted balconied houses and a marina.

half.name: Zarautz
half.blurb: A Basque surf town with one of the region's longest beaches and a historic center dating to medieval fishing days.

half.name: Getaria
half.blurb: A fishing village built on a small peninsula, birthplace of designer Cristóbal Balenciaga and known for grilled turbot restaurants.
